title: The Catalyst for the July Revolution

scenes.speaker: Narrator
scenes.dialogue: On 1 July 2024, students gathered on campuses across Bangladesh, including Dhaka University, for calm demonstrations. These protests had just resumed. At this early stage they were peaceful, a long way from the violent crackdown that would come later in July.

scenes.speaker: Narrator
scenes.dialogue: The trigger sat a few weeks earlier. In June 2024, the High Court reinstated a 30 percent government-job quota reserved for descendants of freedom fighters, reversing a 2018 decision that had abolished it. In a country with high youth unemployment, students read the ruling as a narrowing of merit-based opportunities.

evidence.title: A Student Joins the Movement
evidence.sourceCaption: The Christian Science Monitor, "Bangladeshi youth bore the brunt of last week's violent protests. They want accountability," published and updated 26 July 2024. Paraphrased reporting, not a direct quote.
evidence.text: Prapti Taposhi, an economics student at Jahangirnagar University, was among the first students to join the July 2024 protests over the reinstated government job quota.

evidence.title: University Teachers' Rally at Aparajeyo Bangla, Dhaka University
evidence.sourceCaption: DU News file coverage of the Dhaka University Teachers' Network solidarity rally, July 2024. Original archive filename: teacherPart.jpg. From the chapter-01 source archive, alongside Manab Zamin file footage of the same day's student march. Permission status: pending — academic project, no formal grant obtained.
evidence.archiveNote:
University teachers from institutions across Bangladesh united under the Dhaka University Teachers' Network to express solidarity with students participating in the quota reform movement. During a demonstration held at the foot of the Aparajeyo Bangla sculpture on the Dhaka University campus, the academics called for an immediate end to the violence, forced disappearances, mass arrests, and systemic harassment directed at student demonstrators. Observing a moment of silence to honor those killed, the educators advocated for labeling the deaths as the "July killings" and urged immediate accountability for all parties responsible, including law enforcement and institutional leadership.

Throughout the rally, faculty members strongly criticized the government's autocratic measures and the criminalization of student dissent, characterizing the student movement as a legitimate, historic struggle against long-standing administrative and political repression in higher education. They demanded the unconditional release of detained students, the withdrawal of false charges, and a prompt restoration of an open, safe academic environment so students can safely return to their studies and the democratic process.
